issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may interfere in a criminal appeal under its exceptional appellate jurisdiction when concurrent findings of guilt result in a grave miscarriage of justice through misreading or disregard of material evidence.
material_facts: The appellant appealed by special leave from a conviction affirmed by the High Court.
The courts below convicted the appellant despite evidence that the Supreme Court found insufficient and despite material evidence undermining the prosecution case.
The prosecution case against the appellant depended on circumstantial evidence, including testimony the Supreme Court found too infirm to safely rely on.
issues.conclusion: The Court rejected the contention that it should not interfere with the concurrent findings, set aside the conviction, and acquitted the appellant.
issues.legal_principle: Article 136 of the Constitution confers a wide, overriding power that is ordinarily exercised sparingly in criminal appeals. The Court may intervene to further justice when a judgment has caused a grave miscarriage of justice through a misapprehension or mistake in reading the evidence, or by ignoring material evidence.

predicates.criminal_special_leave_appeal: The proceeding is a criminal appeal brought by special leave.
predicates.concurrent_findings_of_guilt: The trial court and the appellate court both found the accused guilty.
predicates.grave_miscarriage_from_misreading_or_ign: The findings resulted in a grave miscarriage of justice because material evidence was misread or ignored.

issues.definition: When a criminal special-leave appeal challenges concurrent findings of guilt that caused a grave miscarriage through misread or ignored evidence, the appellate court intervenes.

issues.legal_issue: A conviction based on circumstantial evidence cannot stand unless the established circumstances point to guilt and exclude every reasonable possibility of innocence.
material_facts: The appellant was convicted of abetting a dacoity and murder, although the courts below did not find that he was one of the dacoits.

The prosecution relied on alleged enmity, the supposed purpose of the crime, an alleged sighting of the appellant with armed men before the crime, an alleged false alarm, and the appellant’s report to the police after the crime.
The Supreme Court found that the alleged circumstances were not established or were not sufficiently cogent; it also found the testimony supporting the alleged sighting unreliable.
Even assuming the appellant had been seen near the grove, that fact did not establish that he abetted the crime or exclude a reasonable possibility of innocence.
issues.conclusion: The circumstantial evidence did not satisfy the required standard; the conviction was set aside and the appellant was acquitted.
issues.legal_principle: Under Hanumant v. The State of Madhya Pradesh, [1952] S.C.R. 1091, the circumstances from which guilt is inferred must first be fully established, must be conclusive and consistent only with guilt, and must form a complete chain that leaves no reasonable ground for a conclusion consistent with innocence. This standard applied to the charge under sections 396 and 109 of the Indian Penal Code. Suspicion or conjecture cannot replace proof.

predicates.circumstantial_case_alleging_aiding_or_e: The case alleges that the accused aided or encouraged an offense and relies on circumstantial evidence.
predicates.circumstances_not_fully_established: One or more circumstances relied on to infer guilt were not established by the evidence.
predicates.reasonable_possibility_of_innocence_rema: The established circumstances leave a reasonable possibility that the accused was innocent.

issues.definition: In a circumstantial case alleging that an accused aided or encouraged an offense, the accused is acquitted when circumstances are not fully established or a reasonable possibility of innocence remains.
